description.p: Linksy connects your computer and phone directly over your own network. No account, no cloud, no server: what you share goes straight from one device to the other.

ul.li: Send files and folders, or drop them anywhere in the window
Send your clipboard to another device
See and control another computer's screen, or watch your phone's
Use a tablet or phone as a second display
Use your phone's camera as a webcam in any app
Open links from your phone, see its battery, and ring it to find it
Control this computer's music from your phone; calls pause it
Import your phone's photos automatically
Use your phone as a touchpad, keyboard and presentation remote
Browse a folder of your phone in the Files app
Ping a device, and see everything you shared as a timeline

description.p: Pair once by scanning a QR code. Devices nearby show up on their own, and connect only when there is something to share, to save battery.

description.p: Taps on a scaled KDE second display land where you tap, the cursor shows at once after a tap on a still screen, and Linksy reconnects far sooner after a network switch. The service uses about a quarter less memory at rest, and less still until a device can reach it from away or after big transfers.

Transfers like on the phone: a page with the speed, each file and its progress, a panel in the corner on every page, and Send Files and Add Device together at the bottom of your devices. A phone can ask to pick which screen it sees.

Always Allow: a device of yours can see and control this screen without asking each time, from its prompt or a switch on its page; Linksy still tells you when it starts. Taps on KDE's extended screen land where you tap when the display is scaled, paired devices no longer stay "not nearby", and the packages install one file at a time.

Wi-Fi Direct: big files go straight from your phone to this computer over a Wi-Fi link of their own, at about 80 MB/s, four times faster than through the router, while the computer stays on its network (with the Linksy for Android update). Transfers are steadier on busy Wi-Fi.
A paired phone can now follow and set this computer's volume (with a phone app update). The tray menu's icons are one colour, like the rest of the top bar.

Linksy sits in the system tray on every desktop that has one, with your devices and what they can do in its menu. Cover art from browsers reaches the phone, and the phone camera's driver is really rebuilt with the enrolled Secure Boot key.

Second Display works on KDE, at the size KDE gives its virtual monitor, and the phone's pointer reaches the screen's edges there. Keys held from the phone are released when it disconnects, and the phone camera's driver is rebuilt with the Secure Boot key already enrolled.

Second Display goes through the graphics chip when it can encode video, at up to 60 frames a second with almost no processor. On Fedora with AMD graphics, Finish Setup adds the full driver this needs.

Second Display is smooth when Linksy runs as a service: screen sharing gets a memory limit of its own instead of the service's small one. A second display that froze after changing GNOME's display settings now starts again by itself, and screen helpers no longer outlive a crashed service.
Second Display is smooth on laptops without a hardware video encoder: 30 frames a second, and sharp.
Second Display no longer lags on computers without a hardware video encoder: it runs at up to 30 frames a second on several processor cores. In the Flatpak, Save Logs now includes the service's log.
After Update Now, Linksy starts again by itself. What's New lists the highlights of every version since the one you last used, each under its own heading.

Linksy runs on more computers: Ubuntu 24.04 and Linux Mint 22, and Hyprland, Sway, niri and X11 desktops, with a second display on Hyprland and Sway, the installed screen locker for Lock When Away, and Finish Setup that knows what these desktops lack. On public Wi-Fi Linksy no longer announces the computer's name. Files sent together ask once, and Always Accept saves a device's files without asking. Save Logs gathers what's needed for a bug report.

Plugging a phone in to charge no longer asks anything: Connect by USB Cable uses the cable when you want it, and a phone can be set to use it automatically. In the Flatpak, Finish Setup gives the one command that adds the webcam for every app, and the USB guide the one for the cable. Second Display says clearly when the desktop can't make a virtual monitor (Hyprland, Sway) instead of failing.

Update in one click: when a new version is out, Update Now downloads it, checks it against the release, installs it with one password and starts Linksy again. In a terminal, linksy upgrade does the same, and linksy --version and --revision tell exactly which Linksy this is.

Each update now shows what it brings the first time it opens. Installing Linksy always brings its window: the service package now comes with the GTK app, or the Plasma app when that's the one chosen. Answering a request in a notification or in the app takes the notification away.

A Linksy for KDE Plasma: the same app made with Qt and Kirigami, in Breeze. Packages are now split into the service and tools, and the app for your desktop. You can use a relay you host yourself. The phone's camera works on CachyOS and other Arch-based kernels, where Finish Setup now installs the right headers and the camera tool.

Linksy is open source, under the GNU AGPL v3.0 or later. There is an .rpm for openSUSE, and Finish Setup knows openSUSE, including Aeon, Kalpa and MicroOS. Controlling the computer from the phone works again when the remembered screen choice went stale, and screen sharing works on Intel Kaby Lake GPUs. openSUSE no longer asks for the administrator's password at every start, and opening the firewall works with firewalld 2.x.
The phone's camera shows in OBS's camera source and other PipeWire apps by name, not as a blank entry.
A phone whose Linksy app doesn't take the USB cable is no longer switched again and again; the Connect by USB Cable guide says what happened.

Linksy speaks ten languages, the same as Linksy for Android. A Connect by USB Cable guide walks through using a phone over a cable. The microphone card shows a live level with Listen and Stop. Finish Setup installs what's missing on KDE and other desktops too, with one password.
Updating from Linksy 0.6.0 or older now restarts the old background service, so the new version's features show at once.
The terminal is set up from the phone's page, in a card that says what's next. Preferences always open, even right after an update.

Terminal from your phone: a shell on this computer, behind a code you set, allowed per phone, ended from either side. Set Up Everything: Finish Setup checks the firewall, autostart and screen sharing too, and fixes it all with one password.
Received files go to Downloads/Linksy by default. The device page fits any window size.
The screen viewer explains a black status bar when watching some Android phones, and how to fix it on the phone.

A redesigned device page: battery ring, a big Send Files area, one-click tiles, Use As cards for display, webcam and microphone, and a filterable activity timeline. The device list can shrink to a strip of pictures (F9).
Updates take effect right away: the background service restarts into the new version instead of running the old one until you log out.

Away from home: paired devices reach each other over the internet, end-to-end encrypted, for a week after they were last on the same Wi-Fi; screens, files, camera and microphone stay local unless allowed. Locate your phone. 1080p webcam. Linksy is now freeware.
A phone's camera can be used at 60 frames per second.
Linksy tells you when a new version is out, offers to reconnect a second display that dropped, and asks again when remote control wasn't allowed.
Use a phone as a microphone, connect it with a USB cable for lower latency, control its camera from the computer, and see device pictures. The webcam shows up about 0.4 seconds sooner.
Copied images and files go to the other device's clipboard, and text copied here can reach a phone on its own (not on GNOME).
A phone used as a second display gets a monitor in its own shape, filling its screen.
Only what each device can do is offered; a phone's shared folder is named in Files.
Finish Setup installs what features need in one click, and the phone's camera now shows up in browsers and Zoom too.
Flatpak: fewer permissions.
Your phone in the Files sidebar: browse it like a USB drive.
Texting from the desktop: read and send your phone's text messages.
Use your phone as a touchpad, keyboard and presentation remote.
Photo auto-import: your phone's new photos land in your Pictures folder.
Lock When Away: this computer locks itself when your phone leaves.
Music and videos here pause while you're on a phone call, and resume after.
Media controls both ways: your phone's music in GNOME's media controls, and this computer's music on your phone.
Using a phone as a second display no longer shows a black screen.

ul.li: Your phone's notifications on this computer, with Reply
The background service quits right away when asked
Your phone's battery level, with a heads-up when it runs low
Ring your phone to find it, even on silent
Open on PC: links shared from your phone open in this computer's browser
Use as Webcam works in OBS and other apps that pick a camera's format
The Flatpak starts its background service by itself, and at every login
Now also as Flatpak, .deb and .rpm packages
Screen windows fit the shared screen's shape, with no black bars
Preview a device's camera right in the app
Clearer messages when the other device can't do something yet
Closing Linksy never hangs on a device that went quiet
